verse.text: But thou, O LORD, art a shield for me; my glory, and the lifter up of mine head.
verse.summary: David wrote this psalm running for his life from his own son Absalom, with his throne gone and a crowd saying, "There is no help for him in God." That is the posture of a man whose head is down — in grief, in shame, in defeat. Yet in the same breath he calls God his shield, his glory, and the One who lifts his head. If you are walking with your eyes on the ground today because of what happened or what people are saying, let the Lord put His hand under your chin; He is not finished with you, and He will lift your head again.

sermon.title: When I Fall, I Shall Arise
sermon.excerpt: The enemy laughed when you went down, and some of the fall was your own fault. Micah doesn't deny either one — he just refuses to stay on the floor: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.

bibleStudy.title: Make Me a Cake First

verses.text: And the word of the LORD came unto him, saying, Arise, get thee to Zarephath, which belongeth to Zidon, and dwell there: behold, I have commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee. So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, the widow woman was there gathering of sticks: and he called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink. And as she was going to fetch it, he called to her, and said, Bring me, I pray thee, a morsel of bread in thine hand. And she said, As the LORD thy God liveth, I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse: and, behold, I am gathering a few sticks, that I may go in and dress it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die. And Elijah said unto her, Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son. For thus saith the LORD God of Israel, The barrel of meal shall not waste, neither shall the cruse of oil fail, until the day that the LORD sendeth rain upon the earth. And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah: and she, and he, and her house, did eat many days. And the barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Elijah.

And it came to pass after these things, that the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, fell sick; and his sickness was so sore, that there was no breath left in him. And she said unto Elijah, What have I to do with thee, O thou man of God? art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance, and to slay my son? And he said unto her, Give me thy son. And he took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into a loft, where he abode, and laid him upon his own bed. And he cried unto the LORD, and said, O LORD my God, hast thou also brought evil upon the widow with whom I sojourn, by slaying her son? And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the LORD, and said, O LORD my God, I pray thee, let this child's soul come into him again. And the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived. And Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the chamber into the house, and delivered him unto his mother: and Elijah said, See, thy son liveth. And the woman said to Elijah, Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth.

But I tell you of a truth, many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land; But unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow.

bibleStudy.excerpt: Elijah showed up in a famine and asked a widow down to her last handful of flour to feed him first — and the miracle that finally convinced her wasn't the flour staying full, it was her son coming back from the dead.
body: Start in a famine, because that is where every detail here gets its weight. Elijah has just spent months by a brook called Cherith, fed by ravens on a schedule nobody could draw up a budget for, and now the brook has done what brooks do in a drought: it has dried up completely. So the word of the Lord sends him somewhere no sane strategist would choose — not deeper into Israel where the covenant people live, but out past the border to Zarephath, a town that belongs to Zidon, pagan territory, and tells him God has "commanded a widow woman there to sustain thee." She has not been told. Nobody has handed her a memo. When Elijah finds her at the city gate she is doing the smallest, saddest chore in the Bible — gathering two sticks — to cook the last meal she and her son will ever eat before they starve. That is the entire resume of the woman God is about to use to keep His prophet alive.

Watch the order of Elijah's request, because the order is the whole sermon. He asks for water first — fine, reasonable, any traveler would ask that. Then he asks for bread, and when she tells him the truth about her pantry, he does not back off. He doubles down: "Fear not; go and do as thou hast said: but make me thereof a little cake first, and bring it unto me, and after make for thee and for thy son." First. Not after you've fed your boy. Not after you've secured your own house. First, to a stranger, out of the last handful of flour you own. Here's my real question for you today: when the barrel is almost empty, who gets fed first in your house — you, or the word God just put in front of you? Elijah isn't testing her generosity for sport. He's showing her, before she can see it any other way, that obedience is the only door this miracle has.

Notice she doesn't lie to make herself sound more faithful, and she doesn't exaggerate to make herself sound more desperate either. She just tells the prophet exactly what she has: "I have not a cake, but an handful of meal in a barrel, and a little oil in a cruse." That's it. That's the whole inventory. She names the math of her own funeral out loud — gathering sticks "that we may eat it, and die" — and then, in the very next verse, with that math still true, she goes and does it anyway. "And she went and did according to the saying of Elijah." The miracle had not happened yet when she obeyed. The flour had not multiplied yet when she baked. Faith, in this story, is not a feeling that shows up after the evidence arrives. Faith is lighting the fire under an empty-looking pot because a man of God told you to, before you've seen a single extra spoonful.

And then heaven starts paying out exactly the way it said it would — not in a lump sum, but on a schedule. "The barrel of meal wasted not, neither did the cruse of oil fail, according to the word of the LORD." Read the tense carefully: this isn't one dramatic refill. It's "she, and he, and her house, did eat many days" — morning after morning, the same jar, somehow never quite empty. God did not drop a warehouse of grain on her doorstep and let her manage the surplus. He kept doing the miracle daily, which, if you think about it, requires more of Him than one big check would have, and more trust from her than one windfall ever could. Most of us pray for the windfall. God, more often, is in the business of the barrel that just never quite runs out — a much better test of whether you actually believe Him, because you have to come back to that jar hungry every single day.

Just when the story looks finished, it turns, and it turns hard. The boy she just watched God keep alive through a famine gets sick and dies in her arms — "his sickness was so sore, that there was no breath left in him." And this woman who obeyed instantly with her last handful of flour does not respond to this with calm, composed faith. She turns on the prophet: "What have I to do with thee, O thou man of God? art thou come unto me to call my sin to remembrance, and to slay my son?" That is grief talking, not doctrine, and I love her for it. Scripture doesn't sand down her honesty to make her a better poster for faith — it lets her accuse the very man whose instructions kept her fed. You can obey God with your last handful of flour and still, months later, be furious at Him with your whole chest. Both of those are true of the same woman in the same chapter.

Elijah doesn't argue with her grief and doesn't rebuke it. He just takes the boy. He carries him up to the loft, lays him on his own bed, and does something that should slow you down: he cries out to the Lord, then stretches himself over the child's body — not once, but three times — and asks God for one specific thing: "let this child's soul come into him again." Three times he presses his own body over a dead child's body, like a man physically refusing to let go until heaven answers. And "the LORD heard the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived." This is the same prophet who, one chapter earlier, kept a jar of flour going for weeks. Apparently sustaining a widow's pantry and raising her son from the dead both came out of the same obedience — he just didn't know in advance which miracle a given day would require of him.

Here is the sentence that tells you which miracle actually converted her: not the flour — the resurrection. "And the woman said to Elijah, Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth." Now. After weeks of a barrel that never ran dry, she still needed this. I don't think that's a knock on her — I think it's just how we're built. A sustaining miracle, the kind that quietly keeps your lights on and your fridge stocked, gets filed under relief, maybe gratitude, rarely revelation. It takes a resurrection-grade miracle — the thing that was supposed to be permanent getting reversed — before most of us say out loud, now I know. If God has been keeping your barrel full for months and you still haven't said it, don't feel behind. The bigger miracle you're waiting to say it over might already be on its way up the stairs.

Now step into a synagogue in Nazareth, thirty-some generations later, and watch Jesus hand His own hometown a sentence they did not come to hear. He reminds them whose daughter this story really belongs to: "many widows were in Israel in the days of Elias, when the heaven was shut up three years and six months, when great famine was throughout all the land; but unto none of them was Elias sent, save unto Sarepta, a city of Sidon, unto a woman that was a widow." Sit in that for a second. There were other widows. In Israel. In the covenant. In the very same famine. Hungry the same way, entitled by birth the same way — and Elijah was sent to exactly none of them, only to the one woman outside the fence who baked the cake first. Jesus's hometown liked Him fine until that sentence. By the end of the chapter they are trying to throw Him off a cliff. Nothing enrages a comfortable room faster than finding out the miracle was never about proximity.

So here's my real question for you today, the one this whole chapter is actually asking: are you one of the many widows sitting inside Israel, close to the covenant, close to the prophet, close to everything you think should qualify you — and still waiting? Or are you willing to be the one outside the fence who gets the cake made first, the flour that never runs out, and eventually the dead raised, simply because you obeyed a hard word before you saw a single reason to? God was never rationing His miracles by your zip code, your church attendance, or how long you've been sitting in the building. He was watching for who would bake the cake first. Take your handful of meal, your little oil, your situation that looks good for one last meal and nothing more, and do exactly what the word says before you do anything else with it. Your barrel is not too empty for Him. It was never about how much you had. It was always about whether you would go and do according to the saying, in Jesus' name, amen.

lines: Father, I declare today that my fall is not my finish!
Let no enemy rejoice over me — when I fall, I shall arise!
The floor is not my address. I am getting back up!
When I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me!
I will not make my home in the dark place. Your light has found me here!
You are my shield, my glory, and the lifter up of my head!
I own my mistakes, but my mistakes do not own me!
Jesus Christ the righteous pleads my cause before the Father!
You will bring me forth to the light, and I shall behold Your righteousness!
Save this. Speak it over your house today. Knocked down is not knocked out — when I fall, I shall arise! In Jesus' mighty name, amen!

dreamFire.title: The Chase Is Over
dreamFire.intro: Tonight's shield prayer is not aimed at one dream scene — it meets every spirit assigned to chase you, corner you, trap you, or hunt you down between sleep and waking, wherever the pursuit led and whatever shape the hunter wore. Pray it aloud before you close your eyes, and let every chase end before it starts, in Jesus' name.
points: Father, Your Word declares in Psalm 124:7, "Our soul is escaped as a bird out of the snare of the fowlers: the snare is broken, and we are escaped" — every snare spread for me in a dream tonight, every net set to close around me while I sleep, is broken before it closes, and I escape every trap untouched, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the command of Proverbs 6:5, "Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler," I deliver myself tonight from every hunter assigned to chase me, corner me, or run me down in the dream realm — every hand stretched out to hold me finds nothing but air, in the name of Jesus!

Father, Psalm 91:3 promises, "Surely he shall deliver thee from the snare of the fowler, and from the noisome pestilence" — I stand on that surely tonight; every trap laid by a dream-hunter is a trap You have already promised to spring empty, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I cry with David in Psalm 7:1, "O LORD my God, in thee do I put my trust: save me from all them that persecute me, and deliver me" — every power that pursues me through dream after dream, chasing me from street to street, from room to room, is stopped now and cannot land its blow, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, by the word of Nahum 1:8, "...darkness shall pursue his enemies," I reverse the chase tonight — every power that turned itself into my pursuer in a dream is turned into Your prey, and the darkness it hid in now hunts it down, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I decree by Deuteronomy 28:7, "The LORD shall cause thine enemies that rise up against thee to be smitten before thy face: they shall come out against thee one way, and flee before thee seven ways," — every pursuer that rose against me in the night comes one way and scatters seven ways before me, in the name of Jesus!

Father, Isaiah 41:12 declares, "Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, even them that contended with thee..." — every hunter that went looking for me in the dream realm tonight searches and finds nothing, for I am hidden where no contender can reach me, in the mighty name of Jesus!

By the authority of Joshua 23:10, "One man of you shall chase a thousand: for the LORD your God, he it is that fighteth for you, as he hath promised you," I decree that I am no longer the chased but the one who chases — every power that hunted me in dreams past is now put to flight before me, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, Your Word in Psalm 34:7 declares, "The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them" — let angels encamp around my bed tonight, a ring no hunter can cross, delivering me the instant any danger draws near, in the mighty name of Jesus!

I take refuge in Psalm 27:5, "For in the time of trouble he shall hide me in his pavilion: in the secret of his tabernacle shall he hide me... he shall set me up upon a rock" — every chase assigned to wear me down in the dream realm ends at a hiding place no pursuer can find, high upon the Rock, in Jesus' mighty name!

Father, by Exodus 14:14, "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace," I lay down every struggle tonight — You fight every chase, every trap, every pursuit assigned against me while I simply rest, in the name of Jesus!

I stand on Psalm 17:8, "Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings" — every circle of hunters that surrounds me in a dream tonight is broken by the wings that already cover me, and I am too precious to be caught, in Jesus' mighty name!

So I decree over tonight, standing on Psalm 118:6-7, "The LORD is on my side; I will not fear: what can man do unto me?... The LORD taketh my part with them that help me: therefore shall I see my desire upon them that hate me" — no hunter overtakes me, no snare holds me, no chase outruns the One who fights for me; I rise in the morning free, untouched, and unafraid, in the mighty, all-consuming name of Jesus Christ, amen! 🔥
